findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the exact string with `where(email: email)`, and BlockedEmail neither downcases nor strips the address before saving or lookup. A blocked address such as bad@spam.com can therefore be resubmitted as Bad@Spam.com or with surrounding whitespace and miss the block, while the case-insensitive portions of Discourse treat those as the same email. The unique database/model check is likewise case-sensitive, so differently-cased duplicates of a blocked address can coexist. Normalize with the same email downcasing used elsewhere on both record creation and lookup (and ideally a case-insensitive uniqueness guarantee).

findings.title: Validation performs a database write, so match statistics are counted repeatedly
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block? during validation, and should_block? increments and saves match_count/last_match_at. Validation is not a one-time commit event: UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save (which validates again), so one blocked signup attempt increments the counter at least twice, and any other code that merely calls valid?/save on a user with a changed email also records a 'match' even if the user is never persisted. Move the accounting out of the predicate/validator or make it happen once per create attempt; a validator query should be side-effect free.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads a value, increments it in memory, and writes it back. Two concurrent registration attempts matching the same blocked email can read the same count and both save count+1, losing an increment, and the full-record save can also overwrite concurrent changes to fields such as action_type. Use an atomic database increment (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter or a single UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) for the statistics update.

findings.title: The new email validator never checks that the value is an email address
findings.body: EmailValidator.validate_each only applies the whitelist/blacklist domain settings and the BlockedEmail check; it contains no format check. Since User now relies on `validates :email, email: true` (app/models/user.rb:47) as its email validator, a direct API request with a malformed value such as 'not-an-email' passes server-side validation as long as it is present and unique, creating an account whose activation/welcome mail can never be delivered. Add a format validation (using the project's existing email format rules) before the domain/blocked checks.

findings.title: Specs stub out the integration they are meant to prove
findings.body: The validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and calls validate_each directly on a fabricated user, while blocked_email_spec tests BlockedEmail in isolation. Nothing exercises the full path that a User with a real blocked email fails to save through `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so a broken validator registration, autoload problem, or email_changed? condition would let blocked signups through while all new specs still pass. Add a User-level example (and a whitelist/blacklist example for the logic moved out of User) that saves/validates against a real BlockedEmail record without stubbing.
